content: Vaccines work by teaching your immune system to recognize and fight dangerous invaders before an infection ever occurs. They introduce a harmless version of a pathogen—such as an inactivated virus, a fragment of its outer coating, or instructions for making one of its proteins—into your body. Your immune system responds as if it were facing a real threat: specialized cells identify these foreign markers, called antigens, and mount a defense, producing antibodies and activating white blood cells designed to destroy anything carrying those markers. Crucially, your immune system also creates memory cells, which remain in your body long after the vaccine's contents are cleared away. These memory cells act like trained sentinels, ready to respond rapidly if you ever encounter the actual pathogen. Because of this preparation, your body can mount a faster, stronger defense—often preventing illness entirely or significantly reducing its severity, all without you having to get sick first.

content: Vaccines work by teaching the immune system to recognize dangerous invaders before an infection ever happens. They introduce a harmless version of a germ, such as an inactivated virus, a fragment of its surface, or genetic instructions for building that fragment, into the body. The immune system responds as if a real threat had arrived: specialized cells identify the foreign material, and white blood cells called B cells produce antibodies designed to match it. Crucially, the immune system also creates memory cells, which remain in the body long after the vaccine material is cleared. These memory cells stand ready to mount a rapid, powerful response if the actual pathogen appears later. This is why vaccinated people often avoid illness entirely, or experience much milder symptoms, when exposed to the real disease.

Each vaccine contains a harmless version or piece of a pathogen, such as an inactivated virus, a fragment of its protein, or genetic instructions that tell your cells to make that fragment. When this material enters your body, your immune system responds as if it were facing a real threat. Specialized cells called antigen-presenting cells capture the foreign material and display it to other immune cells, triggering a coordinated response. Your body then produces antibodies and activates white blood cells trained to recognize that specific pathogen. Crucially, your immune system also creates memory cells, which can remain in your body for years or even decades. If you later encounter the actual pathogen, these memory cells respond quickly and powerfully, often eliminating it before you feel sick or spread it to others.
